summary: Describes an SMIv2 MIB for devices that implement the Differentiated Services architecture, for monitoring and configuration. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This is a control panel for how a router handles priority traffic.

questions: how to configure diffserv with snmp
what is a rowpointer in snmp
subtitle: An SNMP MIB that lets managers monitor and configure how a router classifies, meters, marks, drops, queues and schedules packets.

tldr.problem: A router or switch that supports the Differentiated Services Architecture needs a standard way for network managers to see and set its per-packet treatment, but the architecture does not say how an implementation is assembled.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB models the data path as separate elements (classifiers, meters, actions, queues and schedulers) held in SNMP tables. Elements are chained together with RowPointer links, and shared parameter tables hold the details such as token bucket settings.
tldr.outcome: The same objects can be used read-only for monitoring or read-create for configuration. Because RowPointers can point into other MIB modules, new elements can be added without changing this one.

today: RFC 3289 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an SNMP companion to the Differentiated Services Architecture of RFC 2475.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3289 describes an SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information version 2) MIB for a device that implements the Differentiated Services Architecture. A MIB is the virtual information store that the SNMP management framework reads and writes. This one can be used both for monitoring and for configuring a router or switch capable of Differentiated Services functionality.

The module is rooted at diffServMib, registered as mib-2 97. A companion module, diffServDSCPTC at mib-2 96, defines the textual conventions Dscp (an integer from 0 to 63) and DscpOrAny, which adds the value -1 as a wild card meaning any value.
sections.eli5: It is a standard list of knobs and dials that lets a manager look at, and change, how a network box treats important and unimportant traffic.

sections.title: Relationship to the Informal Model and Policy
sections.content:
The design is similar to the Informal Management Model for a Differentiated Services router, but it can build data paths that the model describes poorly. The model groups elements into Traffic Conditioning Blocks (TCBs) and cascades them. The MIB does not use TCBs. It links the individual elements directly by following their "Next" attributes.

Each interface and direction (ingress or egress) has a starting point in a data path table. The MIB separates the structure of a policy (do this, then do that) from the parameters it uses. A service provider offering three contract varieties can configure three parameter elements once, and every data path can refer to them. Reusing structural elements is not generally recommended, because it also reuses their counters and loses monitoring detail.
sections.eli5: The recipe (what happens in which order) is kept apart from the measurements (how much, how fast). That way you can write one set of measurements and use it in many recipes.

sections.title: The Data Path and RowPointer Links
sections.content:
When traffic arrives at an interface, the diffServDataPathTable says what happens first. It is indexed by interface and direction, and its entry is a single RowPointer to the first functional data path element. If the start is undefined or zeroDotZero, no specific policy applies.

RowPointers are used in two ways. As a "next" link, a RowPointer says what happens next to classified traffic, to traffic that conforms to a meter, or to traffic that does not. As a "specific" link, it points to the parameter entry that gives the details. A dangling RowPointer or zeroDotZero normally means the data path ends and the traffic goes to the next logical part of the device, such as forwarding or transmission.

Since a RowPointer can point to an entry in any MIB, new elements and new kinds of filter, meter or scheduler can be defined in other modules without changing this document.
sections.eli5: Each station has a little arrow saying "after me, go to that station". Because an arrow can point to a station somebody else built, you can add new stations later.

sections.title: Classifiers and Meters
sections.content:
A classifier is made of classifier elements. Each element has a precedence, a "specific" pointer to the rule, and a "next" pointer for matching traffic. Separate elements for AF11, AF12 and AF13 can feed the same meter. If the "specific" pointer is zeroDotZero, the device is misconfigured and the element is treated as if it were not present.

The one filter defined here is the Multi-field Classifier. It can match an IP source prefix, an IP destination prefix, an IPv6 Flow ID, the IP protocol, TCP/UDP/SCTP source and destination port ranges, and a DSCP. The Behavior Aggregate filter is the special case where only the DSCP is given.

A meter entry has three RowPointers: "succeed" for conforming traffic, "fail" for non-conforming traffic, and "specific" for the parameters. Only token bucket parameters are defined, in diffServTBParamTable, which addresses several modes of the single rate and two rate three color markers (srTCM and trTCM). A token bucket with N rates has N+1 possible outcomes, so multi-rate meters chain entries through the "fail" link in increasing rate order.
sections.eli5: A sorter looks at each letter and decides which pile it belongs to. A counter then checks whether a pile is arriving at the agreed speed, and sends it one way if so and another if not.

sections.title: Actions, Dropping, Queues and Schedulers
sections.content:
Actions are chained through diffServActionNext and end at zeroDotZero, a queue, or another element. The MIB defines a count action (packet and byte counters, useful for billing or analysis), a mark action that sets a DSCP, and an algorithmic dropper. A dropper with alwaysDrop discards everything, while other algorithms normally drop only a few percent of packets at most. The random dropper table carries Active Queue Management parameters such as minimum and maximum thresholds, a maximum drop rate, a sample weight expressed over 65536, and a sampling rate.

The queue table models simple FIFO queues, and the scheduler table builds hierarchies from them. Minimum rate and maximum rate tables attach rates (absolute or as a fraction of interface speed) or priorities to queues and schedulers. A priority scheduler gives a queue the whole interface capacity less what higher priorities use. Weighted schemes such as WRR and WFQ use the minimum rate as the weight, and a maximum rate lets an input act as a non-work-conserving shaper.
sections.eli5: After sorting and counting, stations can count, stamp, or throw letters away. Then letters wait in lines, and a boss decides which line goes first or how much each line gets.

sections.title: Worked AF and EF Examples
sections.content:
The RFC builds an example with one EF class and four AF classes. For each AF class, a Two Rate Three Color Meter splits traffic into groups that conform to both rates, only the higher one, or neither. Two meter entries are chained, and counting and marking actions follow. The first R bits per second are marked AFm1, the next S-R bits per second AFm2, and the rest AFm3.

For EF, a Single Rate Two Color Meter needs one token bucket. Conforming traffic is counted and marked with the EF DSCP, and excess traffic is sent to an alwaysDrop dropper. On egress, AF queues use a rate-based scheduler such as WFQ or WRR with random dropping, and EF uses a priority queue to minimize induced jitter. The two schedulers are cascaded.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows a full setup: ordinary mail gets three speed tiers and a fair share of the trucks, while express mail has a strict limit and always goes first.

sections.title: Row Creation and Compliance
sections.content:
Many tables use an arbitrary integer index unique across the agent. To help several managers create rows safely, each such table has a NextFree object that supplies an unused index, with zero meaning no more entries can be configured. A manager whose row creation fails must re-read it and try again. Each table also has a RowStatus column.

Writing a RowPointer to a row that does not exist returns inconsistentValue. Destroying a row that is still pointed to returns no error but leaves the row intact, and the agent should remove it once nothing refers to it.

The module defines two compliance statements: full compliance for implementations with read-create support, which can be monitored and configured, and read-only compliance for those that can only be monitored.
sections.eli5: When two helpers want to add a new station at once, a numbered ticket machine gives each a different number. If you try to remove a station still in use, it stays until nobody needs it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Anything that can be configured can be misconfigured, with potentially disastrous effects. The MIB has many read-write and read-create objects, so SET operations in a non-secure environment can harm network operations. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 over earlier versions for configuration, in particular the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model.

Some objects may be sensitive from a business perspective because they can reveal a customer's service contract or the filters a provider applies. No objects are sensitive in their own right, such as passwords or monetary amounts. The RFC says it may be important to control even GET access and possibly to encrypt values in transit.
sections.eli5: The control panel can change how the whole network behaves, so only the right people should be able to look at it or turn its dials.

layers.label: Data Path
layers.detail: diffServDataPathTable: starting point per interface and direction

layers.label: Classifier
layers.detail: Selects traffic with classifier elements and filters

layers.label: Action
layers.detail: Count, mark a DSCP, or drop

layers.label: Algorithmic Dropper
layers.detail: Tail, head, random or always drop

layers.label: Scheduler
layers.detail: Priority, WRR or WFQ with min and max rates

items.label: other
items.desc: A dropping algorithm not otherwise listed.

items.label: tailDrop
items.desc: Drops arrivals when the queue reaches its threshold depth.

items.label: headDrop
items.desc: Drops from the head of the queue.

items.label: randomDrop
items.desc: Active Queue Management; parameters come from the random drop table.

items.label: alwaysDrop
items.desc: Drops every packet, as used for excess EF traffic.
